patches.name: Component
patches.summary: Runs a group of patches you built once, with its own inputs, outputs, and memory everywhere you use it.
patches.docs:
## How it works
A component is a group of patches you build once and reuse, like a function. Publish the inputs and outputs you want to reach from outside, then add a Component patch wherever you need that behavior.

- **Ports** are the component's published inputs and outputs, so every Component patch for one component has the same ports.
- **Each instance remembers on its own.** Two Component patches for a press effect animate their own buttons independently.
- **Edits apply everywhere.** Changing a patch inside updates every instance. To vary something per instance, publish it as an input.
- **Defaults.** An input you leave unset uses the component's default.
- **Loops.** Each published input has a Loop Behavior. **Loop** (the default) runs one copy per item, each with its own memory. **Pass** runs one copy and hands it the whole loop. Outputs from several copies join into one flat loop.

## Tips
- Select patches and choose Create Component (⌃⌘G). Cables that crossed the selection's edge become published ports.
- Need each copy's position in a list? Publish an Index input and connect the loop's Index.
- Double-click a Component patch to open its component, and press ⌥↑ to go back.

## Coming from Origami
Published ports live in the component's interface instead of purple and blue port patches, there's no unlink step, and published ports don't carry min and max limits yet.
patches.behavior:
Stateless itself: an instance stores no values of its own. Every patch inside keeps its own state, keyed by (instance scope, copy index, inner patch id, loop index), so each instance and each copy remembers separately.

**Compile.** A `component` patch names a `patchComponent` in the node field `node.component` (not a setting). The engine inlines that component's patches into the host graph, recursing into nested instances:
```
compileInstance(hostScope, hostComponentId, instanceId, node):
  C = doc.components[node.component]
  if (!C || C.kind !== "patchComponent" || wouldCreateComponentCycle(doc, hostComponentId, C.id)) → inert (Edge cases)
  scope = `${hostScope}/${instanceId}`                      // e.g. "main/save_press"
  add hidden node `${scope}/$copies`, fed by the drivers of every published input whose loopBehavior is "loop"
  for each inner patch p: add node `${scope}/${p}`, which also depends on `${scope}/$copies`
  inner input { link: "$in.key" }        → edge from the instance's published input `key`
  host input  { link: "instanceId.key" } → edge from `${scope}/<patch>.<port>`, where C.interface.outputs[key].link is "<patch>.<port>"
```
- Order: topological order runs on the flattened graph, so values cross the boundary in both directions with no delay, and grouping patches into a component doesn't change when values arrive. A host feedback path from an instance output back into one of its inputs is a cycle like any other: the edge that closes it reads the previous frame (ARCHITECTURE.md §5.2), though the delay can land on a different edge than before grouping. An instance output wired straight into the same instance's input is a self-edge and is rejected.
- The generic per-index rule (ARCHITECTURE.md §4) doesn't apply to the instance node: copies, below, replace it.

**Published inputs.** Each frame, for each key in `C.interface.inputs`:
```
value(key) =
  node.inputs[key] is a link    → the source value, coerced to port.type at the boundary (ARCHITECTURE.md §4)
  node.inputs[key] is a literal → the decoded literal
  otherwise                     → the decoded interface default, else the zero value of port.type (CONVENTIONS.md §8)
```
Changing an interface default reaches every instance that doesn't set its own value.

**Copies (loops).** An absent `loopBehavior` means `"loop"`.
```
looping = published inputs with (loopBehavior ?? "loop") === "loop" whose value this frame is a Loop
if (looping is empty)                   { copies = 1; replicated = false }
else if (any looping Loop has 0 items)  { copies = 0; replicated = true }
else                                    { copies = max(items.length over looping); replicated = true }
copy k (0 ≤ k < copies) sees:
  a looping input → items[k % items.length]     // shorter loops wrap
  a "pass" input  → the value unchanged           // a Loop stays a Loop
  a scalar        → the scalar                    // broadcast
```
- Evaluate each flattened inner node for k = 0…copies−1 before moving to the next node. Inside copy k, patches follow the normal per-index loop rules on the values they see. `ctx.loopIndex` and `ctx.loopCount` are their own indices, never k. `ctx.componentPath` is `scope` when not replicated and `${scope}#${k}` when replicated.
- Nested instances replicate inside each copy, so copies multiply and their outputs flatten one level at a time.

**Published outputs.** For each key in `C.interface.outputs`, once the inner nodes it reads have evaluated:
```
v_k = value of the linked inner output in copy k, or the zero value of port.type when `link` is unset
output(key) = replicated
  ? Loop(concat over k of (isLoop(v_k) ? v_k.items : [v_k]))   // flat: loops of loops never form
  : v_0                                                         // scalar or Loop, as produced
```
- A replicated instance always outputs Loops: one copy gives a one-item loop, and zero copies give an empty loop.
- An output linked to `$in.key` passes that input through, per copy.

- Pulses: a `pulse` published input delivers an upstream pulse to its inner consumers on the same frame. A boolean wired into it becomes a pulse on its false→true edge at the boundary, so a held `true` fires once. Inner patches read it with `ctx.pulsed` as usual, and pulses on consecutive frames each count. A `pulse` published output fires on the frame its inner source pulses; when replicated, it is a loop that is `true` only at the copies that pulsed. The boundary adds no same-frame precedence of its own; the inner patches define it.
- Frame 0: inner patches evaluate with authored values and follow their own frame-0 rules (CONVENTIONS.md §16.2). A copy that appears later starts the same way: history seeds from its first value, and animations start at rest on their first target.
- Loops: copy k keeps its state while k < copies. When copies shrinks, the removed copies `dispose` and drop their state; new copies start fresh. Copy 0 of a replicated instance shares state with the unreplicated instance, so an input changing from a scalar to a one-item loop resets nothing. Copies and flattened outputs obey the engine's 10,000-item loop limit and raise its loop-limit issue.
- Variables: local variables inside the component resolve within each copy. Global broadcasters in ancestors are visible inside, and a global broadcaster inside with the same name and type overrides them for this instance and its nested instances (CONVENTIONS.md §18.5.10). A copy's receivers read that copy's broadcaster. Values that arrive through variables never create copies.
- Edge cases:
  - No `component`, a missing component, a component that isn't a `patchComponent`, or an instance that would make a component contain itself: the instance is inert. Nothing inside compiles, every output emits the zero value of its type, and host inputs linked to outputs that don't exist read their own defaults. Raise one runtime issue per restart using the matching diagnostic code (`missing_component`, `component_not_found`, `wrong_component_kind`, `component_cycle`), and never throw.
  - Stored inputs whose key isn't in the interface are ignored at runtime and kept in the file, where diagnostics report them.
  - A literal that no longer fits a retyped published input is coerced to the new type; when coercion fails, the interface default applies.
  - The boundary never produces NaN or ±Infinity. Inner patches apply their own finite-value rules.
- Muted: no inner patch evaluates, no side effect runs, and every inner state is kept, so the component resumes where it left off. Each published output passes through the first published input of the same type, in key order (the order the inspector lists them). Other outputs emit their zero value, and pulse outputs never fire.
- Disabled: there's no built-in `enabled` port. Publish a boolean input and wire it to the inner patches' `enabled` ports.
- Evaluation: the instance does no work of its own. Inner patches keep their own `alwaysEvaluate` flags and `requestNextFrame` calls, and an engine with dirty tracking treats the instance as live while any inner patch is.
- Platform and simulation: works everywhere. Each inner patch keeps its own status, platform rules, and simulation behavior.
- Scripts: a JavaScript patch inside a component uses one script for every instance, so editing it updates them all, while each instance and copy runs its own script state.
- Restart and dispose: restart resets every inner patch in every copy by its own rule. Removing the instance, changing its `component`, or disposing the runtime calls `dispose` on every inner patch in every copy (sockets, audio, timers). On `updateDocument`, inner patches whose id and type are unchanged keep their state in every instance and copy; added patches start fresh and removed ones dispose.
- Coming from Origami: "Loop the Component" is `loop` and "Pass into Component" is `pass`. An absent `loopBehavior` means `loop`, matching Origami v82 and newer; files saved by v81 or older defaulted to Pass, so importers write `pass` explicitly for them. The purple and blue published-port patches (`builtin.group.input`, `builtin.group.output`) become interface entries and `$in` / output links, not patches. Local component ids (`com.facebook.local.<n>`) and vendored library components import as `component` patches when they hold only patches, and as `componentInstance` layers when they hold layers. Port Setup's min and max have no interface field yet, so importers drop them. Origami doesn't document evaluation order across the boundary; Sonobe flattens so a component never adds latency.
patches.dynamicPortsRule:
Ports come from the component named by `node.component` (a `PatchNode` field, not a setting). Core already implements this rule: `COMPONENT_PATCH_SPEC.dynamicPorts` calls `componentInterfacePorts` in `packages/core/src/registry.ts`.
- Inputs: one per entry in `interface.inputs`, sorted by key: `{ key, name: name || key, type, default: the decoded interface default (omitted when absent), enumOptions: the option keys, each used as its own name, description: "Published input \"<name>\"." }`.
- Outputs: one per entry in `interface.outputs`, sorted by key, with the same shape and no default.
- Keys are the interface keys exactly as stored (`^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$`, the id rule), so imported components keep keys like `Start_Value`. This is an exception to the camelCase port-key rule (§6.1), because the component's interface is the source of truth. Authors should still keep keys unique across inputs and outputs; links resolve because a link's side is always known.
- `loopBehavior`, `category`, and `link` don't create ports. `category` groups ports in the inspector.
- No `component`, or a component that doesn't exist: no ports. Stored inputs stay in the file and raise diagnostics until the component exists again.
- Editing the interface regenerates the ports of every instance. `updateInterface` merges ports by key (`null` unpublishes one); with `replace: true` each side it's given is the whole set, and keys it leaves out are unpublished. Removing a published input disconnects instance inputs with that key and host links that read it off a layer instance (`@chip_1.label`), and removing a published output disconnects host links from instance outputs with that key; the op's inverse restores both (`updateInterface` in `packages/core/src/ops/components.ts`). Renaming a key is a remove plus an add, so its cables must be reconnected. Changing `name` or `type` keeps cables; a type change can leave links that diagnostics flag as mismatched. An output declared again without `link` keeps its inner cable; `link: null` disconnects it.
- Creating: `createComponent` with only `patchIds` makes a `patchComponent`. It publishes one input per distinct outside source, typed from the inner port it feeds, and one output per inner output read outside, then leaves a `component` patch wired the same way.
commonMistakes: A looped component gives one result instead of one per row: its input's Loop Behavior is Pass, so a single copy runs and patches like Loop Count see the whole loop. Set that input to Loop to run one copy per item.
Changing a value inside the component changed every button: all instances share the component's patches. Publish that value as an input, then set it on each Component patch.

An output has 25 items for a 5-row list: each copy produced a loop of 5, and copies join into one flat loop. Reduce each copy's loop to one value inside the component, for example with Loop Any or Loop Sum.

examples.title: Reuse one press effect on two buttons
examples.description: Both buttons use the Press Feedback component. Each instance runs its own spring, and the Cancel button sets Depth to press deeper than the default.
examples.outline:
component main "Main" (prototype)
layer save_button rectangle "Save Button" @24,720 160x56 cornerRadius=28 scale←save_press.scale
layer cancel_button rectangle "Cancel Button" @218,720 160x56 cornerRadius=28 scale←cancel_press.scale
patch touch_save interaction layer=@save_button
patch touch_cancel interaction layer=@cancel_button
patch save_press component component=press_feedback down←touch_save.down
patch cancel_press component component=press_feedback down←touch_cancel.down depth=0.9

component press_feedback "Press Feedback" (patchComponent)
input depth number "Depth" default=0.95
input down boolean "Down" default=false
output scale number "Scale" ←shrink.output
patch pop popAnimation number←$in.down bounciness=0 speed=20
patch shrink transition<number> progress←pop.output start=1 end←$in.depth

examples.title: Let each heart in a row remember its own like
examples.description: Tap uses Loop behavior, so the component runs one copy per heart, and each copy's Switch remembers whether that heart is liked.
examples.outline:
component main "Main" (prototype)
layer heart oval "Heart" position←grid.position size←grid.size scale←like.scale
patch rows loop count=3
patch grid gridLayout index←rows.index columns=3 origin=40,400 width=322 itemHeight=88 spacing=24
patch tap_heart interaction layer=@heart
patch like component component=like_toggle tap←tap_heart.tap

component like_toggle "Like Toggle" (patchComponent)
input tap pulse "Tap" loop=loop
output liked boolean "Liked" ←toggle.on
output scale number "Scale" ←grow.output
patch toggle switch flip←$in.tap
patch pop popAnimation number←toggle.on
patch grow transition<number> progress←pop.output start=1 end=1.2
